text: CHAPTER 1: INTRODUCTION
1. BACKGROUND
i. The Problem of Secrets in Logs

Modern cloud-native applications generate very large volumes of log output, and developers routinely, and almost always accidentally, place sensitive credentials in that output. Common examples observed in production logs include a database connection string logged at debug level that contains a username and password, an authentication-failure log that includes the full Authorization header carrying a bearer token, an informational log line that echoes a configured payment-provider secret key, and a debug dump of the process environment that exposes cloud access keys. The weakness is catalogued as CWE-532, the insertion of sensitive information into a log file [1], and the OWASP logging guidance lists passwords, access tokens, connection strings and encryption keys among the data that must be excluded from logs [2].
ii. Where a Leaked Secret Goes

A secret written to a log does not stay where it was written. It flows through a log-shipping agent such as Fluent Bit [3] into an aggregation platform such as Loki, Elasticsearch, Datadog or Splunk, where it persists for months or years and remains readable by any engineer who holds log-query permission. It is then copied into backups, dashboards and exports. By the time someone notices the exposure, it has already occurred, and the remedy is no longer to delete a line but to rotate a credential everywhere it may have been used. Figure 1.1 contrasts the same log line before and after LogShield.
Figure 1.1: Before and after: secret redaction in action
iii. The Gap in Existing Tooling

Research has shown that credential leakage is a widespread and continuing problem in public source repositories [4], and has produced labelled datasets for evaluating secret detectors [5]. That work, and the tools built on it, concentrate on source code and git history. The log stream that a running application produces is a separate leakage channel. No open-source, runtime engine that sanitises this stream inside the workload was found in the literature and tooling reviewed for this project, and this is the gap that LogShield addresses.
2. MOTIVATION

The motivation for LogShield follows from the observation that existing categories of tooling address the problem too late, too far from the point of leakage, or not at all. Git history scanners such as Gitleaks, TruffleHog and detect-secrets [6, 7, 8] operate on code and commit history, so the secret has typically already been committed, and in the logging case already shipped, before they act. Secrets managers such as HashiCorp Vault and AWS Secrets Manager [9, 10] prevent credentials from being hard-coded, but they do not intercept a credential that an application accidentally logs. Runtime security tools such as Falco [11] detect behavioural anomalies but are not designed to inspect or sanitise log content. Cloud scanners such as Datadog Sensitive Data Scanner, Amazon Macie and Google Sensitive Data Protection [12, 13, 14] are, in their cloud mode, applied after the data has been sent to the provider; Datadog’s own documentation states that in this mode the data leaves the environment before it is redacted [12].

A related motivation, raised explicitly during project review, is that a system combining detection, recovery and lineage tracking must be positioned honestly against prior art and not claimed as unprecedented. Point solutions already exist for individual pieces of this problem. Real-time, in-pipeline masking exists: Datadog’s Observability Pipelines Worker redacts or hashes sensitive data inside the customer’s infrastructure before logs are shipped onward [15], and CloudWatch Logs data protection policies mask matching values [16]. Secret fingerprinting and reuse detection exist for source code [17, 7]. Encrypted storage with audited, role-gated retrieval exists in secrets managers [9, 10]. What was not found is a single open-source component that unifies detection, encrypted recovery and lineage tracking at the point where an application log line is about to leave its pod. That unification, and not any single mechanism in isolation, is the scope this project occupies. Figure 1.2 shows the points in a secret’s life at which each category of tool acts.
Figure 1.2: Where existing tools act, and the point at which LogShield intercepts (Datadog SDS shown in cloud mode)
3. OBJECTIVES
The objectives of the project, stated as outcomes that can be checked, are as follows.
To intercept, sanitise and vault a secret before the log line exits the pod, with zero network dependency and no change to application code.

To compute a multi-signal Secret Confidence Score (SCS) from 0 to 100, using pattern match, entropy, variable-name proximity, structural validation, context and encoding signals, and to resolve it through three decision gates: MASK, FLAG and PASS.
To keep per-line latency within a sub-5-millisecond design target while sustaining thousands of lines per second on a single sidecar.

To retain each masked value only in an encrypted local vault, retrievable by reference ID through a role-gated command-line interface that writes an audit trail and deletes entries after a time-to-live.
To detect reuse of the same secret across pods and namespaces by a keyed-hash (HMAC) fingerprint, without storing a second plaintext copy.
To deploy with zero configuration for developers: labelling a namespace should cause a mutating admission webhook to inject the sidecar automatically.
To evaluate the system empirically with a labelled benchmark, a root-cause analysis of false positives, an enumeration of engine edge cases and a four-way ablation experiment on a 50,000-line corpus.
4. SCOPE OF THE PROJECT
i. In Scope

The delivered core comprises the sidecar entry point and the LogMask detection engine with its pattern catalog of more than 600 hand-crafted detectors, the SecureReveal encrypted vault and its command-line interface, the SecretLineage HMAC fingerprint tracker, a demonstration application that leaks secrets on purpose, a benchmark suite, a weight-training script and Kubernetes deployment and RBAC manifests. The ten-week plan in Chapter 3 extends this core with the 761 SecretBench patterns, an explicit multi-stage pipeline, machine-learned weights, an Aho–Corasick prefilter, an active validity analyser, vault hardening, a mutating admission webhook, Prometheus metrics and an enterprise dashboard.
ii. Out of Scope

The project does not include an eBPF kernel hook, AI-based detection beyond the logistic-regression confidence model, PII policy engines or organisation-wide policy management, a centralised cross-cluster lineage aggregator, or a SIEM platform itself (only an audit exporter is planned). Production-grade certificate automation for the webhook is limited to what the demonstration deployment needs. These items are recorded as future work in Chapter 7. Table 1.1 summarises the boundary.

text: 5. OVERVIEW OF THE PROPOSED SYSTEM

LogShield is a Kubernetes-native sidecar that implements a six-stage, multi-factor detection pipeline producing a Secret Confidence Score on a scale of 0 to 100. The score is resolved through three decision gates, shown in Table 1.2.
Table 1.2: Secret Confidence Score decision gates

data: Redact the value, encrypt it in the local vault, and record a lineage fingerprint
Mark the value with a reference ID without redacting it

text: The system is organised around three modules. LogMask is the detection engine and the most technically substantial component. Instead of the naive regex or keyword matching used by most existing tools, it computes a multi-signal confidence score from the entropy of a candidate string, its proximity to trigger words such as “password”, “token” or “secret”, its match against known credential formats such as AWS keys or JWTs, and contextual cues such as debug-level logging. SecureReveal is the vault and controlled-recovery module: encrypted storage, reference IDs, role-based retrieval, audit logging and TTL-based auto-deletion, following the standard secrets-management pattern. Its specific contribution is the integration of the vault with the redaction pipeline, not the vault mechanism itself. SecretLineage is the fingerprinting and tracking module. It detects reuse of the same secret across applications, without storing the plaintext again, by means of a keyed hash (HMAC) fingerprint.

In operation, the application writes its log output to a volume shared with the sidecar. The sidecar tails the file, passes every line through LogMask, and only then writes the resulting, possibly redacted, line to standard output, where the cluster’s existing log-shipping agent collects it as usual. Masked values are simultaneously written to the vault and fingerprinted. The deployment principle is zero configuration for application developers: labelling a namespace with logshield.io/enabled=true causes a mutating admission webhook to inject the sidecar together with its shared volumes, after which logs are redacted without any change to application code. The design is described fully in Chapter 4.

text: 7. ORGANISATION OF THE REPORT

Chapter 2 surveys the existing landscape of secret-detection tooling and the building blocks used, and states the gap the project occupies. Chapter 3 defines the problem, lists requirements, states the threat model and explains the proposed solution and the development methodology. Chapter 4 presents the architecture, the detection pipeline, the confidence model, the data design and the deployment design. Chapter 5 reports the results obtained from the implementation completed to date, including the module inventory, benchmark results, false-positive analysis and implementation status. Chapter 6 describes the testing strategy, the edge-case analysis and the planned validation. Chapter 7 concludes, states advantages, limitations and applications, and sets out future work. References and appendices follow.
